etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From earlier len (with excrescent -d, as in sound, round, etc.), from Middle English lenen, lænen, from Old English lǣnan (“to lend; give, grant, lease”), from Proto-West Germanic *laihnijan, from Proto-Germanic *laihnijaną (“to loan”), from Proto-Germanic *laihną (“loan”), from Proto-Indo-European *leykʷ- (“to leave, leave over”).

Cognate with Scots len, lend (“to lend”), West Frisian liene (“to lend, borrow, loan”), Dutch lenen (“to lend, borrow, loan”), Danish låne (“to lend, loan”), Swedish låna (“to lend, loan”), Icelandic lána (“to lend, loan”), Icelandic léna (“to grant”), Latin linquō (“quit, leave, forlet”), Ancient Greek λείπω (leípō, “leave, release”). See also loan.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To allow to be used by someone temporarily, on condition that it or its equivalent will be returned.

quote.citation: 2013 June 1, “End of the peer show”, in The Economist, volume 407, number 8838, page 71:
quote.text: Finance is seldom romantic. But the idea of peer-to-peer lending comes close. This is an industry that brings together individual savers and lenders on online platforms. Those that want to borrow are matched with those that want to lend.

definitions.definition: (reflexive) To be suitable or applicable, to fit.
To afford; to grant or furnish in general.

quote.citation: 1712 (date written), [Joseph] Addison, Cato, a Tragedy. […], London:  […]  J[acob] Tonson, […], published 1713, →OCLC, Act I, scene ii, page 1:
quote.text: Cato, lend me for a while thy patience.

quote.citation: 1886, John Addington Symonds, Sir Philip Sidney:
quote.text: Mountain lines and distant horizons lend space and largeness to his compositions.

quote.citation: 2019 June 8, “Condemning the return to premiership of General Prayuth Chan-ocha through a manipulative method”, in forsea.co‎[1], FORSEA, retrieved 2019-06-09:
quote.text: FORSEA absolutely condemns the political manipulation on the part of the junta, General Prayuth, the Thai Senate and the parties that lent their support for General Prayuth that led him to parliamentary victory.

quote.citation: c. 1800s, Arthur McBride, version from 2012, Dick Sheridan, Irish Songs for Ukulele (Songbook), Hal Leonard Corporation (→ISBN):
quote.text: “But,” says Arthur, “I wouldn't be proud of your clothes, / For you've only the lend of them, as I suppose.”
Yesterday asked Mr. Aray the lend of 8s. 6d. for a month.

Somehow, Joe managed to talk his way out of trouble. 'I told him I was getting the lend of them,' Joe laughed. It wasn't only vegetables that were targeted, though. For generations of children who grew up on ...

quote.text: Our thanks go to Diran Adebayo for his support, especially his lend of Everything You're Told Is True, to the website. It has been an honour to host  […]

quote.citation: 2016, Mary Peters, Betsy, The Coalminer's Daughter, New Generation Publishing, →ISBN:
quote.text: “Give these to your dad, Betsy, tell him thanks for the lend of them. I'm leaving next week, Betsy.” “Really, where are you going?” Betsy played dumb.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English lende (usually in plural as lendes, leendes, lyndes), from Old English lendenu, lendinu (“loins”), plural of Old English lenden (“loin”), from Proto-West Germanic *landī, from Proto-Germanic *landį̄ (“loin”), from Proto-Indo-European *lendʰ- (“loin, kidney”). Cognate with Scots lend, leynd (“the loins, flank, buttocks”), Dutch lendenen (“loins, reins”), German Lenden (“loins”), Swedish länder (“loins”), Icelandic lendar (“loins”), Latin lumbus (“loin”) (whence loin), Polish lędźwie (“loins”), Russian ля́двея (ljádveja, “thigh, haunch”).

definitions.definition: (anatomy, UK dialectal) The lumbar region; loin.
(UK dialectal, of a person or animal) The loins; flank; buttocks.
